As freight demand is projected to grow significantly, there is an urgent need to address the environmental impacts of rail transportation to meet near-term and long- term regulatory emission reduction goals and to improve local air quality. 1.2 RATIONALE FOR USING BIOFUELS The U.S. rail sector requires exploring viable alternatives to conventional diesel fuel for energy security, air pollution reduction, and diversification of fuel choice perspectives. Alternative fuels, particularly biofuels, offer promising solutions for several reasons: • Compatibility with Existing Infrastructure: Several biofuels can be used in current locomotive engines with minimal modifications, enabling a more straightforward and cost- effective transition. • Immediate Impact: Biofuels can reduce lifecycle emissions in the near term, without waiting for the locomotive fleet to turnover and to be replaced with new propulsion and/or energy conversion technologies. • Renewable Resources: Biofuels are produced from renewable feedstocks such as agricultural residues and energy crops, contributing to energy security and diversifying our domestic energy sources • Reduced Criteria Air pollutant (CAP) Emissions: Advanced biofuels and other alternative fuels can, in some cases, also reduce the CAP emissions. • Support for Rural Economies: Biofuel production can stimulate economic growth in rural areas through feedstock cultivation and processing. • Divert Organic Waste Streams: Biofuel production can reduce the landfilling of human, animal, and other organic wastes; this reduces costs for their disposal while also generating a revenue stream. Biofuels can be a solution, providing immediate emission reductions and energy securities while other technologies, such as electrification and hydrogen fuel cells, continue to develop and mature. 1 1.3 BIOFUEL OPTIONS CONSIDERED IN THIS REPORT This study focuses on seven alternative fuel options, that are of interest to the relevant stakeholders in the U.S. rail sector, including renewable diesel (RD), biodiesel (BD), bio-oils, ethanol, methanol, dimethyl ether (DME), and ammonia. Numerous feedstocks and conversion technologies can be used to produce these alternative fuels. An initial screening was conducted to identify the promising feedstocks and conversion pathways for each alternative fuel, based on technoeconomic analysis (TEA) and lifecycle analysis (LCA) studies available in the open literature, as well as the technology readiness levels (TRLs). Sixteen pathways were considered (Figure 1-1) which covers biochemical, thermochemical, and e-fuel conversion technologies with TRLs >5 and four feedstock types (first-generation biomass, cellulosic biomass, organic waste, and renewable H ). Key objectives include: • Fuel Evaluation and Comparison: Identify and analyze the most promising alternative fuels based on economic, environmental, and scalability factors, assessing their system requirements, fuel blends, infrastructure needs, and potential deployment in alternative fuel corridors.
